intro:
Modernist architecture builds with new construction technology and rejects ornament, so volume, structure and plan carry the whole design. It emerged at the end of the 19th century and was dominant from the Second World War until the 1980s. In 1932 Hitchcock and Johnson's exhibition at MoMA set out its principles: architecture as volume, regularity in the facade rather than symmetry, and no applied ornament. Under the name International Style it spread throughout the world. Le Corbusier's white houses of the 1920s had no ornament inside or out.

The Fagus Factory in Alfeld (1911), by Walter Gropius and Adolf Meyer, sets its glass curtain wall forward of the piers, so the corners turn with no column. Gropius's Bauhaus Dessau (1926) wraps its workshops in glass on a pinwheel plan. Mies van der Rohe's Villa Tugendhat in Brno (1930) brings the open plan into a family home, with glass walls that drop away to the garden. Le Corbusier's Villa Savoye in Poissy (1931) puts his Five Points of Architecture into a single house. Mies's Seagram Building in New York (1958) stands back behind a plaza, its bronze mullions expressing the frame.

intro:
Contemporary architecture is the architecture of the 21st century, from 2000 to today, and no single style leads it. It is shaped by method more than style: new structural systems make buildings taller, lighter and stronger than in the 20th century, and designs are modelled in 3D on computers. Some designers favour natural, ecological materials such as stone, wood and lime; energy efficiency over a building's whole life is a primary goal of sustainable design. The field is global, with important new buildings in China, Russia and India.

The Burj Khalifa in Dubai (2010), once the tallest building in the world, rises on a Y-shaped buttressed core that steps back in a spiral against the wind. Shigeru Ban's Centre Pompidou-Metz (2010) covers three stacked gallery tubes with a woven grid of glued laminated timber. Snøhetta's Oslo Opera House (2008) slopes a marble roof into the fjord, open for anyone to walk on. OMA's CCTV Headquarters in Beijing (2012) joins two leaning towers with a 75-metre cantilever. Herzog & de Meuron's Elbphilharmonie in Hamburg (2017) sets a glass crown on a brick warehouse, with a public plaza between old and new.

intro:
Deconstructivist architecture breaks a building into fragments, with no obvious harmony, continuity or symmetry; its look is often described as controlled chaos. The name plays on Russian Constructivism and on the ideas of the French philosopher Jacques Derrida. The style came to public notice with the 1982 competition for the Parc de la Villette. In 1988 Mark Wigley and Philip Johnson curated an exhibition at MoMA that crystallised the movement and made its seven architects famous: Peter Eisenman, Frank Gehry, Zaha Hadid, Coop Himmelblau, Rem Koolhaas, Daniel Libeskind and Bernard Tschumi. Gehry refused the label, as he refused any other.

Eisenman's Wexner Center for the Arts in Columbus (1989) runs a white steel scaffold grid along two shifted city grids, splitting fragments of a brick armoury. Gehry's Vitra Design Museum in Weil am Rhein (1989) collides white plastered volumes around skylit galleries. In the same town, the Vitra Fire Station (1993), Hadid's first built work, is a set of sharp concrete planes caught in motion. Libeskind's Imperial War Museum North in Manchester (2002) is three fragmented, intersecting curved volumes, shards of earth, air and water from a shattered globe.

intro:
High-tech architecture shows how a building is made and how it works: structure, lifts, stairs and ducts are put on display instead of hidden. It emerged in the 1970s as a form of late modernism and was first developed in Britain. Steel, aluminium and glass dominate. Interiors have no internal load-bearing walls, so the space can be rearranged, and services often move outside into separate towers. The style is used most for factories, offices and galleries, and its leading architects include Hopkins, Foster, Rogers, Piano and Calatrava.

Renzo Piano and Richard Rogers's Centre Pompidou in Paris (1977) moves structure and colour-coded services outside, leaving free floors and a public piazza. Michael and Patty Hopkins's Hopkins House in London (1976) is a two-storey steel and glass box entered by a bridge. Rogers's Lloyd's Building in London (1986) sets lifts, stairs and ducts in plug-in towers around a 60-metre atrium. Norman Foster's HSBC Main Building in Hong Kong (1986) hangs its floors from suspension trusses, freeing a public plaza beneath. In Malaysia, Ken Yeang's Menara Mesiniaga (1992) cools a round tower with spiralling sky gardens and sunshades on its hot facades.

intro:
Postmodern architecture brings back what modernism took out: historical references, ornament, colour and wit. It emerged in the 1960s against the austerity and sameness of modern buildings. Denise Scott Brown and Robert Venturi are credited with introducing it, and Venturi set it out in a 1966 book that declared, "I am for messy vitality over obvious unity." Postmodern buildings borrow historical elements and allusions and use unusual materials. The style is best known in America, but notable examples appeared in Europe, and in the late 1990s it split into many new tendencies.

Venturi's Vanna Venturi House in Philadelphia (1964) splits a gable facade over a broken arch. Charles Moore's Piazza d'Italia in New Orleans (1978) is a public square with a fountain shaped like Italy, curved colonnades and neon. Michael Graves's Portland Building (1982) paints giant pilasters and a keystone onto a cubic block. In Stuttgart, James Stirling's Neue Staatsgalerie (1984) ramps a public path through an open drum courtyard, with a classical plan and pop-coloured details. Philip Johnson and John Burgee's AT&T Building (550 Madison Avenue) in New York (1984) caps a granite tower with a broken pediment.

intro:
Art Deco architecture pairs bold geometry with rich decoration: setbacks, sunbursts, metal ornament and decorated crowns. It first appeared in Paris in the 1910s, just before the First World War, growing from the geometric forms of the Vienna Secession and Cubism. Its name comes from the 1925 exhibition of decorative and industrial arts in Paris. Reinforced concrete gave more freedom of form. It was an international style that flourished in the 1920s and early 1930s, and Miami Beach holds the largest concentration of Art Deco buildings in the world.

Josef Hoffmann's Stoclet Palace in Brussels (1911) is described as a prototype of the style: white marble planes edged with bronze mouldings make its walls read as thin panels. Auguste Perret's Théâtre des Champs-Élysées in Paris (1913) spans its auditorium with a concrete frame behind a flat marble front. In New York, the Chrysler Building (1930) stacks a stainless-steel crown of sunburst arches above its setbacks, and the Empire State Building (1931) was the world's tallest building until 1970. The Palais de Chaillot in Paris (1937) curves two wings around a terrace that opens a view to the Eiffel Tower.

intro:
Art Nouveau architecture takes its lines from nature: the curves of plants and flowers, asymmetry and whiplash lines that give a sense of movement. Architects built it with new materials: iron, glass, ceramics and later concrete. The first Art Nouveau houses appeared in Brussels in the 1890s, and the style spread from Britain, Belgium and France across Europe. In German it is called Jugendstil, after the art journal Jugend. Hector Guimard brought it into public architecture with his entrances for the Paris Métro. By the start of the First World War in 1914 it was largely exhausted.

Victor Horta's Hôtel Tassel in Brussels is a defining example: exposed iron columns and whiplash ornament flow through an open, top-lit stair hall. His Hôtel van Eetvelde (1898) lights the core of a narrow townhouse through an octagonal hall under a glass cupola. Guimard's Castel Béranger in Paris (1898) mixes brick, stone and ceramic around a whiplash-curved iron gate. Otto Wagner's Majolikahaus in Vienna (1899) covers a flat apartment front in weatherproof tiles printed with flowers. Charles Rennie Mackintosh's Glasgow School of Art (1909) sets huge north-light studio windows in a stone front.

intro:
Critical regionalism is modern architecture rooted in its place: it starts from the local topography, climate and light rather than a universal style. The idea was first presented in 1981 by the theorists Alexander Tzonis and Liane Lefaivre, and the historian Kenneth Frampton developed it further. It tries to mediate between the global and the local languages of architecture, and it rejects the whimsy and ornament of postmodernism. It has grown into distinct sub-styles around the world.

Alvar Aalto's Säynätsalo Town Hall in Jyväskylä (1952) gathers brick rooms around a raised grass courtyard, with timber trusses over the council chamber. Álvaro Siza's Boa Nova Tea House in Leça da Palmeira (1963) sets low tiled roofs among the rocks above the sea, reached by steps through the boulders. Jørn Utzon's Bagsværd Church near Copenhagen (1976) hides a billowing concrete ceiling, washed with daylight, inside a plain industrial shell. Geoffrey Bawa's Parliament of Sri Lanka (1982) groups pavilions with stacked copper roofs on an island in an artificial lake. Balkrishna Doshi's Indian Institute of Management Bangalore (1983) links courts and classrooms of rough granite and concrete with long corridors under open pergolas.

intro:
Famous houses by architects are small buildings that carry big arguments. A house can express the opinions of the people who build it or live in it, and its form is shaped by the materials at hand, so a single house can set out a whole way of building. In January 1945 John Entenza's magazine Arts & Architecture announced the Case Study Houses, to produce inexpensive modern model homes that could be built again and again.

Frank Lloyd Wright completed Fallingwater for the Kaufmann family in 1937, with a guest wing in 1939; its concrete terraces cantilever over a waterfall. Le Corbusier built the Villa Savoye in Poissy between 1928 and 1931 in reinforced concrete, putting his Five Points of Architecture into one house; it had an enormous influence on international modernism. Mies van der Rohe's Farnsworth House (1951) is a single glass room lifted above a floodplain on eight steel columns. Charles and Ray Eames built the Eames House in Los Angeles for themselves in 1949 from mass-produced parts. Robert Venturi's Vanna Venturi House in Philadelphia (1964) is one of the first prominent works of postmodern architecture.

intro:
Library architecture has to store books and bring people to them, and over time the balance has moved from archive to public room. The first libraries were archives of the earliest writing, such as the Library of Ashurbanipal in Mesopotamia. As collections grew, libraries ran short of space and introduced compact shelving on tracks. Between 1883 and 1929, 1,689 Carnegie libraries were built in the United States, and the public libraries of the 1960s were shaped by modernism. Today libraries also work as community hubs.

Henri Labrouste's Bibliothèque Sainte-Geneviève in Paris, opened in 1851, leaves its slender cast-iron columns and arches visible over the reading room; it is called a major step towards modern architecture, and it influenced the Boston Public Library, McKim Building (1895). Gordon Bunshaft's Beinecke Rare Book & Manuscript Library in New Haven (1963) filters light through translucent marble panels onto a glass-walled book tower. Toyo Ito's Sendai Mediatheque (2001) carries thin floors on thirteen lattice tubes. OMA's Seattle Central Library (2004) stacks shifted platforms inside a diamond-mesh skin, and its Books Spiral keeps the nonfiction collection in one continuous run.

intro:
A pavilion is a smaller building set apart from, or attached to, a main building, and it was traditionally built for pleasure and relaxation. The word comes from a large tent raised on posts. World's fairs, art biennales and national fairs use national pavilions, and most are temporary, taken down when the fair closes. The Giardini in Venice holds 30 permanent national pavilions, some by leading 20th-century architects. Since 2000 the Serpentine has commissioned a summer pavilion from a leading architect every year.

Mies van der Rohe and Lilly Reich's Barcelona Pavilion (1929) sets free-standing walls under a floating roof, so space flows instead of forming rooms. In Hanover, the Japan Pavilion, Expo 2000 by Shigeru Ban with Frei Otto was a gridshell of recycled paper tubes, designed to be recycled afterwards, while MVRDV's Netherlands Pavilion, Expo 2000 stacked Dutch landscapes, from dunes to a forest floor, into a vertical park. He Jingtang's China Pavilion, Expo 2010 in Shanghai cantilevers an inverted pyramid of red beams modelled on dougong timber brackets. John Nash's Royal Pavilion in Brighton (1823) shows the older meaning: a building for pleasure, crowned with bulbous domes.

intro:
Housing architecture designs homes in numbers, and much of its history is the history of public or social housing: subsidised or affordable homes provided in larger buildings. Modern municipal housing began as a response to fast urban population growth. In Britain, mass council house building began around 1920, after the Addison Act of 1919, and tower blocks followed in the 1950s. Red Vienna placed large blocks around green courts. Le Corbusier's Unité d'Habitation turned housing into a modernist type, with "streets in the sky" and a shared roof terrace.

Bruno Taut and Martin Wagner's Hufeisensiedlung in Berlin (1927) bends a horseshoe of housing around a pond. Karl Ehn's Karl-Marx-Hof in Vienna (1930) runs for over a kilometre around large green courts. The Unité d'Habitation in Marseille (1952) has 337 flats, with internal streets on every third floor and a communal terrace on the flat roof. Park Hill in Sheffield (1961) takes those streets outside as wide concrete decks. Alejandro Aravena's Quinta Monroy in Iquique (2004) builds half a good house and leaves the other half for families to finish; the approach helped Aravena win the 2016 Pritzker Prize.

intro:
Religious architecture designs places of worship, whose plan and form carry belief. Ancient temples were often seen as a god's dwelling. A Hindu temple is read as a model of the universe and of inner space, its sanctum crowned by a tower, the shikhara, called the vimana in the south. The earliest mosques were hypostyle halls with courtyards for Friday prayer, and the Ottomans introduced the central-dome mosque in the 15th century. Gothic architecture began in 12th-century France at the abbey church of Saint-Denis, and its defining feature is the pointed arch. In the 20th century, steel and concrete changed church design.

Hagia Sophia in Istanbul (537) was one of the first buildings with a fully pendentive dome. The Sultan Ahmed Mosque (Blue Mosque), from 1617, rings its central dome with four semi-domes. The Great Mosque of Djenné in Mali (1907) is built of mud brick, its palm-wood beams left as fixed scaffolding for re-plastering. Le Corbusier's Notre-Dame du Haut in Ronchamp (1955) punches thick walls with deep, coloured windows that model the light. Tadao Ando's Church of the Light in Ibaraki (1989) cuts a cross into a concrete wall.

intro:
School and campus architecture matters because the design of a building can strongly shape how students learn. A campus traditionally means the land and buildings of a college or university. In 1922 Patrick Abercrombie contrasted the American campus, its departments scattered about a park among the trees, with the formal quadrangles of Oxford and Cambridge. Gothic, which flourished in English universities from the 13th to the 15th centuries, was later revived for campuses. Brutalism was used on university campuses around the world in the 1960s and 1970s, and in the same years open classrooms became popular in North America. Walter Gropius founded the Bauhaus in Weimar on 1 April 1919.

Gropius's Bauhaus Dessau (1926) wraps the school's workshops in a glass curtain wall on a pinwheel plan. William Pereira's Geisel Library in San Diego (1970) is a campus building of that brutalist era: its reading floors stack outward like an inverted stepped pyramid on splayed concrete piers above a glazed base. Foster + Partners' Apple Park in Cupertino (2017) takes the campus idea into the workplace: a ring of curved glass around a planted courtyard.

intro:
Memorial architecture gives remembering a place: a memorial is an object or place that focuses memory or commemoration. The most common kind is a gravestone or a plaque, and temporary, makeshift memorials are called grassroots memorials. A mausoleum is a monument that encloses a burial chamber; the word comes from the tomb of Mausolus at Halicarnassus. Maya Lin's Vietnam Veterans Memorial, dedicated in 1982, is two black granite walls, and its colour, lack of ornament and form below ground were controversial at first.

Peter Eisenman's Memorial to the Murdered Jews of Europe in Berlin (2005) sets 2,711 concrete stelae on a sloping grid, forming narrow aisles; critics said its lack of names or information weakens its message. Karl Friedrich Schinkel's Neue Wache in Berlin (1818), a Neoclassical guardhouse, is now a memorial lit by an oculus. Anitkabir in Ankara (1953), the mausoleum of Atatürk, leads a ceremonial road lined with lions to a vast court. Mazar-e-Quaid in Karachi (1970) raises a white marble cube with pointed arches on a platform. The Taj Mahal in Agra (1653) sets a white marble tomb on a raised plinth in a quartered garden.

intro:
New York's architecture is worth studying for its skyscrapers: the city has one of the largest and most varied collections in the world. The 1916 Zoning Resolution required setbacks and limited towers to a share of the lot; Art Deco towers such as the Chrysler and Empire State buildings took their tapered tops from those rules. Grand Central Terminal was built in the Beaux-Arts style. Later, the Seagram Building and 330 West 42nd Street became early influential examples of the International Style in the United States.

Cass Gilbert's Woolworth Building (1913) dresses a steel frame in Gothic Revival terracotta. William Van Alen's Chrysler Building (1930), which many historians and architects rank among the city's finest, stacks a stainless-steel crown of sunburst arches above its setbacks. The Empire State Building (1931) was the first building to pass 100 storeys and the world's tallest until 1970. Mies van der Rohe's Seagram Building (1958) stands back behind a plaza, its bronze mullions expressing the frame; the critic Paul Goldberger called it one of the city's most copied. The MetLife Building (1963) sets a precast concrete slab across Park Avenue above Grand Central.

intro:
Chicago is where the skyscraper was worked out, and it holds one of the world's largest and most varied collections. The Great Chicago Fire of 1871 destroyed most of downtown, and the city rebuilt. The Montauk Building (1882–83) was the first to be called a skyscraper, and Jenney's Home Insurance Building (1885) is considered the first with steel in its structural frame. A steel skeleton meant height was no longer limited by the strength of the walls. Louis Sullivan set aside historical precedent to stress height, and from 1963 a "Second Chicago School" grew from Mies van der Rohe's work at IIT.

The Monadnock Building (1893) is the tallest load-bearing masonry building ever built. The Reliance Building (1895) was the first skyscraper with large plate-glass windows over most of its surface. Sullivan's Sullivan Center (Carson Pirie Scott Building), finished in 1907, sets a white terracotta grid over an ornate cast-iron base. Mies's 860-880 Lake Shore Drive (1951) places two steel and glass towers at right angles, their I-beam mullions expressing the frame. Bruce Graham and Fazlur Khan's John Hancock Center (1969) tapers inside an X-braced tube that resists the wind.

intro:
Paris is a city where styles were born and then set into a single, ordered plan. Gothic architecture began in the rebuilding of the choir of Saint-Denis, finished in 1144, and around 1160 Maurice de Sully used it at a far larger scale for Notre-Dame. The city imposed formal height limits on its buildings in 1667. In 1853 Napoleon III made Haussmann prefect of the Seine, starting the rebuilding of Paris; the programme ended when Haussmann was dismissed in January 1870. The world's fairs of 1889 and 1900 added the Eiffel Tower and the Grand Palais, and the design for the Centre Pompidou was chosen from 681 competition entries.

Charles Garnier's Palais Garnier (1875) turns its grand staircase and foyers into a promenade as theatrical as the stage. Gustave Eiffel's Eiffel Tower (1889) gathers four curving wrought-iron legs into a single tapering shaft. Charles Girault's Grand Palais (1900) hides a riveted steel-and-glass vaulted nave behind stone Beaux-Arts facades. Renzo Piano and Richard Rogers's Centre Pompidou (1977) moves its structure and colour-coded services outside, leaving free floors and a public piazza.

intro:
Berlin's architecture is worth studying because the city's 20th century, from Weimar-era reform to the Cold War and after, is written in its buildings. Karl Friedrich Schinkel set its classical core: his Altes Museum, opened in 1830, became a model for national art museums around the world. Seven Weimar-era housing estates by Bruno Taut, Martin Wagner and others now form a World Heritage group that influenced housing far beyond Germany. East Berlin built Karl-Marx-Allee (1949–1960) as a showpiece of workers' housing in socialist classicism, and the Hansaviertel, mostly destroyed in the war, was rebuilt as the Interbau project with Aalto, Gropius, Niemeyer and others. Potsdamer Platz, left desolate in the Cold War, was rebuilt in the 1990s.

Taut's Gartenstadt Falkenberg (1916), nicknamed the paintbox estate, paints its garden-city terraces in strong colours. His Hufeisensiedlung with Wagner (1927) bends a horseshoe of housing around a pond. Norman Foster's Reichstag (1999) tops the parliament with a glass dome whose mirrored cone reflects daylight into the chamber below. Daniel Libeskind's Jewish Museum Berlin (2001) follows a zigzag plan cut through by empty "voids" that visitors can see but not enter.

intro:
Tokyo's buildings share no single style, but the city is a key place to study modern Japanese architecture: it was left in ruins twice in recent history and rebuilt each time. The Great Kanto earthquake of 1923 began an era of concrete building, and an air raid in March 1945 burned much of the city. The 1964 Olympics marked its rebirth. Metabolism was launched with a manifesto for the 1960 World Design Conference in Tokyo, treating the city as a living organism. Kenzo Tange mentored the Metabolists without joining them.

Tange's Yoyogi National Gymnasium (1964), built for the Olympics, hangs a suspension roof from two concrete masts; his Pritzker citation counted it "among the most beautiful buildings of the 20th century". His St. Mary's Cathedral (1964) joins eight concrete shells in a cross-shaped skylight. The Kasumigaseki Building (1968) was Japan's first modern skyscraper, 36 floors on a flexible steel frame built to ride out earthquakes. Kisho Kurokawa's Nakagin Capsule Tower (1972) bolts prefabricated capsules to two cores, the world's first example of capsule architecture. Nikken Sekkei's Tokyo Skytree (2012) damps sway with a concrete core, like a pagoda's central column.

intro:
Barcelona's architecture is worth studying for one plan and one movement. Ildefons Cerdà's Eixample of 1859, the city's biggest expansion, laid a strict grid of wide avenues and square blocks with chamfered corners. Modernisme ran from the city's first World Fair in 1888 to 1911; Antoni Gaudí is its best-known architect, and Lluís Domènech i Montaner created a genuine alternative to his work. For the 1929 Exposition, Mies van der Rohe built the German Pavilion, demolished in 1930 and rebuilt permanently in 1983–86.

Gaudí's Casa Batlló (1906) wraps a bone-like facade around a light well tiled from deep to pale blue to even out the daylight. His Casa Milà (1912) carries an undulating stone facade on columns, with two light courts and a catenary-arched attic. The Sagrada Familia, begun in 1882, filters coloured daylight into its nave through branching, tree-like columns and hyperboloid vaults. Domènech i Montaner's Palau de la Música Catalana (1908) uses a steel frame to open walls of glass and a stained-glass skylight over the concert hall. Mies van der Rohe and Lilly Reich's Barcelona Pavilion (1929) sets free-standing walls under a floating roof.

intro:
Los Angeles architecture is studied above all for its modern houses: the Case Study Houses changed how homes were designed. Arts & Architecture launched the programme in 1945 and asked for houses "capable of duplication", not one-off performances. Rudolph Schindler's house of 1922 was a cooperative live/work space for two young families and set a precedent for California architecture. Frank Lloyd Wright called Hollyhock House his "California Romanza". Googie, the roadside Space Age style, was named after a Hollywood coffee shop. In 1978 the Los Angeles Conservancy was founded to save the Central Library from demolition.

The Schindler House (1922) is built of tilt-up concrete slabs with glass slits, its L-shaped studios each opening onto a garden court. Charles and Ray Eames's Eames House (1949) is a Case Study House assembled from off-the-shelf industrial parts. Pierre Koenig's Stahl House (Case Study House #22), from 1960, cantilevers an L-shaped steel and glass pavilion over the Hollywood Hills; its photograph is one of the most famous of Los Angeles. Frank Gehry's Walt Disney Concert Hall (2003) wraps a vineyard-style hall in curved stainless steel, a cheaper skin than the stone first planned.

intro:
A cantilever is a structural member fixed at one end and free at the other, so a building can overhang with no support underneath. In a traditional timber-framed building, a cantilevered upper floor is called a jetty. Bridges can be built outward from both sides as pairs of cantilevers that meet in the middle.

Frank Lloyd Wright's Robie House in Chicago (1910) projects long roofs from the core of the house instead of resting them on walls. At Fallingwater (1939) he used cantilevers to push large balconies over a waterfall: the concrete terraces are held only at one end, extending outward from the chimney. Giuseppe Pettazzi's Fiat Tagliero Building in Asmara (1938) shapes a service station like an aeroplane, with two 15 m concrete wings cantilevered from a central tower. Coop Himmelb(l)au's Busan Cinema Center (2011) is captioned as having the world's longest cantilever roof, carried on a single cone over an outdoor theatre.

intro:
A courtyard is an area open to the sky, often surrounded by a building, bringing light, air and privacy into the middle of a plan, which people want nearly everywhere. In warm weather an open central court helps cool a house. Courtyard houses go back to the Neolithic, around 6400–6000 BC, and courtyards were widely used in the ancient Middle East. The open centre of a Roman house was called the atrium, and in Morocco's old towns the courtyard house has always been the standard form.

In the Alhambra in Granada the basic unit of the palace is a rectangular courtyard, each room opening to the sky. The Shah Mosque, Isfahan (1629) rings its central courtyard with four monumental iwans. Louis Kahn's Salk Institute in La Jolla (1965) sets its laboratories around a travertine plaza open to the Pacific. Tadao Ando's Row House in Sumiyoshi in Osaka (1976) splits a concrete box with an open courtyard you cross to get to bed, even in the rain. Foster + Partners' Kogod Courtyard, National Portrait Gallery in Washington, D.C. (2007) covers a 19th-century courtyard with an undulating glass canopy.

intro:
A brise-soleil, French for "sun breaker", is a screen that shades a facade and cuts a building's heat gain by deflecting sunlight. The simplest form is a horizontal projection on the sunny side. It is used most on glass facades that would otherwise overheat, and it still lets in the low sun of mornings, evenings and winter. Le Corbusier popularised patterned concrete versions, and Santiago Calatrava designed a moving one shaped like a wing. At the Institut du Monde Arabe, 240 photo-sensitive, motor-controlled apertures act as a brise-soleil.

Lúcio Costa and Oscar Niemeyer's Gustavo Capanema Palace in Rio de Janeiro (1945) sets adjustable brise-soleil on the sun facade of an office slab. Le Corbusier's Palace of Assembly in Chandigarh (1962) is a parliament built for the Punjab sun. His Curutchet House in La Plata (1953) fits house and clinic on a narrow lot behind a brise-soleil. Calatrava's Milwaukee Art Museum, Quadracci Pavilion (2001) opens and folds a winged sunscreen of steel fins above a glass hall. Renzo Piano's New York Times Building (2007) screens clear glass walls with horizontal ceramic rods that shade the offices.

intro:
Timber architecture covers both the oldest ways of building in wood and some of the newest. Mass timber is a class of large engineered wood parts that carry structure. Cross-laminated timber stacks layers of boards at right angles for strength and serves for walls, floors and roofs. Mass timber buildings go up faster than steel or concrete ones and perform very well in earthquakes. The oldest known half-timbered building is in Roman Herculaneum.

The Pagoda of Fogong Temple (Yingxian Wooden Pagoda), from 1056, is the oldest fully wooden pagoda still standing in China, held together without nails by 54 kinds of bracket sets. The Ise Grand Shrine is traditionally rebuilt in cypress every 20 years, which keeps the craft alive. Frei Otto and Carlfried Mutschler's Multihalle Mannheim (1975) is a timber lath gridshell, laid flat and then pushed up into shape. J. Mayer H.'s Metropol Parasol in Seville (2011), marketed as the world's largest wooden structure, spreads timber parasols over a market and Roman ruins. Voll Arkitekter's Mjostarnet in Brumunddal (2019) was the world's tallest wooden building when it was finished, an 18-storey glulam frame.

intro:
A tensile structure carries only tension, with no compression or bending, and it should not be confused with tensegrity. Because tensile structures span long distances economically, they are most often roofs. Pretensioning keeps their flexible parts stiff. Common fabrics are PTFE-coated fibreglass and PVC-coated polyester, and some roofs use ETFE film in single layers or cushions. Vladimir Shukhov was one of the first to calculate their stresses. Frei Otto championed the idea, founded the Institute for Lightweight Structures in Stuttgart in 1964, and first used it for the West German pavilion at Expo 67.

Maciej Nowicki and William Henley Deitrick's J. S. Dorton Arena in Raleigh (1952) was the first structure in the world with a cable-supported roof. Kenzo Tange's Yoyogi National Gymnasium in Tokyo (1964) hangs its roof from two concrete masts. For the Munich Olympic Stadium (1972), Behnisch & Partner and Otto spread a cable-net roof with acrylic glass panels. Richard Rogers's Millennium Dome in London (1999) hangs a PTFE-coated fabric roof on cables from twelve yellow masts. Foster + Partners' Khan Shatyr Entertainment Center in Astana (2010) is a tilted cable-net tent of ETFE cushions.
